If you have been around for the thriving years of the #gischat and NACIS[^nacis]
community on Twitter[^other], you may remember [Joshua Stevens][joshua]'s post 
on [how to make bivariate maps][orig]. Now, eleven years later, Joshua reflects 
back on it and [shares some interesting updates][new]:

> Back then, making bivariate maps meant blending color schemes in graphics 
programs, hand-tuning the corner where both variables run high, and stitching 
two classifications together into a single attribute your software could 
understand. It worked in any tool, but it took some patience. A lot has changed 
since then.

[![Bivariate choropleth map comparing climate anxiety and risk of climate-related natural hazards (source: Joshua Stevens, Maps.com)](bivariate-map-1500x1000.jpg "Bivariate choropleth map comparing climate anxiety and risk of climate-related natural hazards (source: Joshua Stevens, Maps.com)")][new]

The [post][new] looks at updates to software, workflows, and colour spaces, 
among other things. It is an interesting short read for those interested in 
cartography or more broadly in the evolution of geospatial technology and 
technique.

[joshua]: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jscarto/
[orig]: https://www.joshuastevens.net/cartography/make-a-bivariate-choropleth-map/
[new]: https://www.joshuastevens.net/blog/still-bivariate-still-curious/

[^nacis]: [North American Cartographic Information Society](https://nacis.org/).
[^other]: Or you may have come across it in other ways as well, of course. It 
was very widely shared back then, in my perception.
